In France, the social security system ensures that prenatal and postnatal care in public hospitals is entirely covered. Women who earn wages also receive 16 weeks of maternity leave, with daily compensation ranging from €9.29 ($10.94) to €84.90 ($100), depending on their prior earnings. During pregnancy and the period surrounding birth, financial circumstances remain largely unchanged: families in vulnerable situations continue to face hardship, just as they did before, while affluent families maintain their comfortable standing.

However, when it comes to actual support for new mothers, the picture is bleak — virtually no provisions exist to assist them. Paternity leave is limited to just 11 days, which doesn't even cover the time needed for a mother to physically recover after giving birth. As a result, new mothers are left to handle the relentless demands of their new responsibilities while simultaneously trying to recuperate.

On top of this, they need to find childcare, even though state-provided options fall short of demand, particularly in and around Paris. Childcare expenses fluctuate considerably. At daycare facilities, lower-income families may pay as little as €1,000 ($1,177.59) annually — yet only one slot is available for every eight children needing care. This forces families to turn to private alternatives, like in-home caregivers or childminders.

Any other questions?
